title: Earth-Mars light time and solar conjunction windows, 2026-2029 (JPL Horizons)

source.publisher: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Solar System Dynamics Group
source.name: JPL Horizons On-Line Ephemeris System: observer table, Mars (499) from Earth geocenter (500@399); conjunction threshold calibrated to NASA/JPL command-moratorium announcements
source.license: No data license is stated in the Horizons manual or API documentation (checked 2026-11-14); those pages link the JPL Image Use Policy (https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/jpl-image-use-policy). Horizons was developed at JPL (Caltech) under contract with NASA. Cited per the manual's 'References for the Horizons system'.
source.citation: Giorgini, JD and JPL Solar System Dynamics Group, NASA/JPL Horizons On-Line Ephemeris System, <https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/>, data retrieved 2026-Nov-14. Observer table, target Mars (499), center Earth geocenter (500@399), quantities 20, 21, 23, daily. Accessed through the Horizons API (https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api), signature "NASA/JPL Horizons API" version 1.2.

caveats: Ephemeris output, not a measurement: JPL Horizons observer table for Mars (499) seen from the Earth geocenter (500@399), one sample per day at 00:00 UTC. Interpolate linearly between days.
Range is Earth-center to Mars-center. A ground antenna or a crew on the surface differs by at most about one Earth radius plus one Mars radius (about 0.03 light-seconds).
One-way light time is geometric (range / c with the au and c printed by Horizons). Relativistic (Shapiro) and solar-plasma delays near conjunction are not modelled; both are well under one second.
Up-leg and down-leg light times differ by at most 0.04 s over this span (range-rate bound in data.uplink_vs_downlink_bound_s); the table is the down-leg.

Conjunction windows are a model: the days on which the Sun-Earth-Mars elongation is below one threshold (2.04 deg) fitted to NASA/JPL published command-moratorium dates (RMS edge residual 0.79 d, worst 2.42 d). Real moratoria are operational decisions; NASA wrote in 2021 that a few missions extend theirs 'a day or two in either direction'.
Published moratorium dates carry no time zone; they are compared as UTC calendar days.
The calibration years (2012-12-01..2025-12-31) come from a second Horizons request; it also supplies the December 2025 start of the window that straddles 2026-01-01.
For the January 2026 conjunction NASA published a no-contact span (Dec. 29 - Jan. 16), not a command-moratorium span; it is shown as an out-of-sample comparison and is not part of the fit.

Horizons API documentation states version 1.3 (2025 June) but the API signature returned version 1.2; the parser keys on column names and the $$SOE/$$EOE markers and fails loudly if the format changes.
A planetary ephemeris does not go stale on a clock (stale_after is null): the values are valid until coverage.stop. Past dates in the span are ephemeris reconstructions, not telemetry.

3 of 8 published moratorium quotes were re-verified against the live page in this build; the others could not be fetched by the scripted client (see calibration.published[].quote_verification_note) and rest on a reading of the raw page HTML on 2026-11-14.

from: horizons header: Units conversion: 1 au= 149597870.700 km, c= 299792.458 km/s

au_km.basis: as printed in the Horizons header

column_basis.range_km: derived: range_au x au_km, rounded to 1 km
column_basis.one_way_light_time_s: derived: range_au x light_time_per_au_s, rounded to 1 ms

light_time_cross_check.resolution_note: Horizons prints light time in minutes with 8 decimals (6e-7 s), so agreement at ~3e-7 s is agreement to its last digit.

source.arithmetic: max over rows of |deldot| x one-way light time / c

conjunctions.min_elongation_basis: smallest of the daily 00:00 UTC samples (not a refined minimum)
conjunctions.basis: derived: Sun-Earth-Mars elongation below the calibrated threshold (edges linearly interpolated between daily samples, rounded to the hour)

conjunctions.min_elongation_basis: smallest of the daily 00:00 UTC samples (not a refined minimum)
conjunctions.basis: derived: Sun-Earth-Mars elongation below the calibrated threshold (edges linearly interpolated between daily samples, rounded to the hour)

source.arithmetic: threshold = argmin over {1.00, 1.01, ..., 4.00} deg of the sum, over the 12 start and end dates of 6 NASA/JPL published moratoria, of (computed edge - published day at 12:00 UTC)^2 in days^2; a computed edge is the linearly interpolated time the daily elongation crosses the threshold

calibration.sign_convention: residual = computed edge - published day (12:00 UTC); negative = the model opens or closes the window earlier than NASA did
calibration.date_convention: Published dates carry no time zone or time of day; each is taken as a UTC calendar day and compared at its midpoint, so |residual| <= 0.5 means the computed edge falls on the published day.

cross_check.note: JPL itself printed 'two degrees' (2013 and 2015 releases). It is reported here as an independent check, not used to set the threshold.
